hard_gate_weakening.difference: NEW-for-Ezek PUNCTA arm (U+05C4 valid only at MT 41:20/46:22): a positive claim is accepted whenever ANY verse in the ref's cited RANGE is a true site, with no check that the specific verse number named in the claim's own tail text is one of the two true sites.
hard_gate_weakening.evidence: Empirically confirmed: ref 'web:Ezek.41.1-Ezek.41.26 (puncta at 41:5, single-witness)' (a false claim - 41:5 has no puncta) produced ZERO problems, while the identical false claim narrowed to 'web:Ezek.41.5-Ezek.41.5 (...)' was correctly flagged 'claims puncta extraordinaria but they stand only at MT 41:20 and MT 46:22'. The existing test suite (_test_zone_tools_ezek.py, PUNCTA2_CS) only tests a covering range where the CORRECT number (41:20) is named (cs_puncta_range_ok) - it never tests a covering range paired with a WRONG number, which is exactly the gap.

hard_gate_weakening.difference: The same NEW-for-Ezek PUNCTA arm, structurally identical defect: 'ok = bool(span_sites) or ...' short-circuits on the ROW'S SPAN alone, so any puncta claim in prose passes once the row's span covers a true site, regardless of what verse number the claim's local text actually names.
hard_gate_weakening.evidence: Empirically confirmed: row with span 'Ezek.41.12-Ezek.41.20' (covers the true site 41:20) and prose 'the upper dot U+05C4 puncta extraordinaria appears at 41:5' (a false claim) produced ZERO puncta_claim_in_ezek flags. The same prose with span 'Ezek.40.1-Ezek.40.4' (no true site) correctly flagged puncta_claim_in_ezek three times. The test suite's cm_puncta_span_covers_site_ok vector never pairs a covering span with an explicit wrong number - untested gap.

hard_gate_weakening.difference: NEW-for-Ezek Qere-acceptance branch ('if run in KQ["qere"]') checks a candidate Hebrew run against the CONCATENATION of every Qere reading in the whole book (134 notes joined by ' | '), not against the Qere of the specific verse the run is cited near - unlike citation_sweep.py's Qere arm, which is correctly scoped per-verse via kq.get(vkey).
hard_gate_weakening.evidence: Code: normalize_hebrew_in_json.py build_index() builds one book-wide KQ['qere'] string; fix_string() tests membership in it with no verse-key argument. In practice this tool's stated job is byte-fidelity only (is this Hebrew real, not degraded), and the ref-binding-correctness gate is citation_sweep.py's separately-scoped Qere arm, so a wrong-verse Qere misattribution should still be caught downstream. Real suite run counted 30 real writer quotes accepted via this path with none surfacing as mis-bound in citation_sweep's report, so no live exploitation is confirmed - recorded as a latent scoping looseness, not a demonstrated pass-through.

findings.claim: A structured-ref puncta claim naming the WRONG verse silently passes Tier-0 whenever its own ref range happens to include a true puncta site (MT 41:20 or 46:22), because the check only asks whether the covered SET intersects the two true sites, never whether the claim's own tail number is one of them.
findings.evidence: Private vector 'adv_cs_wrong_verse_number_in_covering_range' (ref 'web:Ezek.41.1-Ezek.41.26 (puncta at 41:5, single-witness)') produced problems=[] and status GREEN-for-this-row; the control vector with the range narrowed to 41.5-41.5 correctly produced the RED problem. Run via PYTHONIOENCODING=utf-8 python citation_sweep.py over a private copy in my own scratch.
findings.how_verified: Executed citation_sweep.py directly (permitted, no --write) on a 2-row private JSONL I authored; compared output JSON.
findings.suggested_fix: In the PUNCTA arm, additionally extract any explicit C:V / C.V number in the claim's own tail (as check_marks.py's PUNCTA_NUM already does) and require that number, under both MT/WEB readings, to be a true site before treating the claim as satisfied by span coverage alone; or require the ref itself to be a single-verse citation for a positive puncta claim.

findings.claim: The identical defect as T1-01: a prose puncta claim naming the WRONG verse silently passes whenever the ROW'S SPAN (not the claim's local context) happens to cover a true site, because 'ok = bool(span_sites) or ...' short-circuits before any local-number check runs.
findings.evidence: Private vector 'adv_cm_wrong_number_span_covers_site' (span 'Ezek.41.12-Ezek.41.20', prose falsely claiming puncta 'at 41:5') produced flag_count 0 for rule puncta_claim_in_ezek; the control vector with span 'Ezek.40.1-Ezek.40.4' (no true site) correctly produced 3 puncta_claim_in_ezek flags for the identical prose.
findings.how_verified: Executed check_marks.py directly (permitted) on a 2-row private JSONL I authored; compared output JSON.
findings.suggested_fix: Require the local PUNCTA_NUM-extracted number (when present) to itself resolve to a true site under either reading before falling back to 'span covers a site' as the sole justification; only use bare span-coverage as the ok-path when no explicit number is present in the local window at all.

findings.claim: PUNCTA_NEG ('\b(?:no|not|nor|without|absent|lacks?|none)\b(?:\s+[\w/-]+){0,2}\s*$') does not model double negation (e.g. 'not without puncta', 'not lacking puncta') and would misclassify an assertion of PRESENCE as a denial, or vice versa for a negation more than two words removed from the puncta mention.
findings.evidence: Regex read: a trailing '...not without ' immediately before the PUNCTA match satisfies the pattern (matches on 'without'), so a double-negation phrase asserting presence would be treated as a denial. This is a false-positive-direction risk (flags a true claim as contradictory), not a hidden-defect-pass risk, and no such phrasing was observed in the real corpus (0 puncta problems/flags of either polarity appear in the shipped suite summary).
findings.how_verified: Static regex analysis only; not exercised against real rows (no matching phrasing exists in the reviewed corpus to test against).
findings.suggested_fix: Low priority given real-corpus absence; if hardened, extend the adjacent-negation window to detect a second negator inside the 0-2 word span and cancel.

findings.claim: The Qere-disclosure check in the Hebrew-quote-binding arm ('if KQ_WORD.search(o)') tests the ENTIRE current prose FIELD for a ketiv/qere keyword, not proximity to the specific Hebrew run being evaluated - a field containing two Hebrew quotes, one legitimately disclosed and one not, could let the second ride on the first's disclosure keyword.
findings.evidence: Code read at citation_sweep.py lines ~404-419: KQ_WORD.search(o) where o is the whole field string. This mirrors a pre-existing, Jer-inherited looseness at the ROW level (kq_web_quote_warn's 'if not KQ_WORD.search(json.dumps(row, ...))' guard, present unchanged in both Jer and Ezek), so it is not a new-for-Ezek regression, but it is a real scope gap worth recording since it is a NEW arm.
findings.how_verified: Static code read only; not exercised (constructing a realistic two-Qere-quote-in-one-field row was out of scope for the time available).
findings.suggested_fix: Scope the disclosure check to a window around the specific run's position, matching the +-120/160 char window convention used elsewhere in the same file and in check_marks.py.

findings.claim: This pre-Tier-0 per-part QC tool's K/Q legitimacy check ('kq_raw = " ".join(n for v in pm["kq"].values() for n in v)') treats every OSHB K/Q note as one undifferentiated whole-book string (ketiv and qere concatenated, never run through ezek_lib.kq_split), which is looser and structurally different from citation_sweep.py's and normalize_hebrew_in_json.py's per-note, split, Qere-only acceptance. This does not weaken the shipped Tier-0 gate (citation_sweep.py's stricter, later check still governs disclosure correctness), but it is an inconsistency across review stages that could confuse a writer about what 'legitimate Qere' means.
findings.evidence: Code read at _validate_writer_part.py lines 74-81, 151-152, contrasted with ezek_lib.kq_split-based logic in citation_sweep.py and normalize_hebrew_in_json.py. The real suite run's defects_listed still caught several whole-note (ketiv+qere concatenated) copies as defects at the Tier-0 stage, confirming the final gate is not weakened by this earlier tool's looseness.
findings.how_verified: Code read only (tool is not on the MAY-run list; not executed).
findings.suggested_fix: Low priority; if normalized, have this tool call ezek_lib.kq_split too, for consistency of the 'Qere' concept across review stages.

answers.q1: Two structural differences carry real risk; the rest are clean mechanical or well-tested adaptations. cap_sweep.py and check_language_zones.py are pure book-token/count substitutions with no behavioral change (verified against their Jer/Lam sources respectively). citation_sweep.py and check_marks.py each add three genuinely NEW-for-Ezek arms (puncta, Qere tier, editorial-note K/Q tier) beyond the carried zone/special-letter/sigla substitutions. The editorial-note K/Q tier and the Qere-disclosure logic are documented, tested, and (for Qere) empirically exercised (30 real acceptances, no observed mis-binding). The PUNCTA arm in BOTH tools is documented and tested, but the tests never cover a wrong verse number embedded in a range/span that happens to include a true site - and I confirmed by direct execution that this exact case passes silently in both tools (T1-01, T1-02). This is the class of defect the brief warned an author who already caught six of its own would produce a seventh of.
answers.q2: Yes to both parts of the question, verified by code trace and execution. A run straddling a ketiv/qere junction, a bare ketiv, or an NFD-only match of a Qere cannot pass citation_sweep's Hebrew-quote-binding arm: byte-tier is required for pointed quotes, the Qere fragment used is the isolated post-split qere half only (never the ketiv or the whole note), and NFD-tier is explicitly excluded from the Qere path (falls through to a hard 'does not collate' failure). A disclosed Qere (KQ_WORD present in-field) always passes; an undisclosed one always fails via the explicit qere_undisclosed branch - confirmed by code trace of citation_sweep.py lines ~404-423. One real scoping looseness: the disclosure check is field-wide, not proximity-scoped (T1-04), and normalize_hebrew_in_json.py's separate Qere-acceptance check is book-wide rather than per-verse (recorded under hard_gate_weakening, unconfirmed as exploitable in practice).
answers.q3: No - confirmed by direct execution that a false claim at the wrong verse CAN pass in both tools, whenever the ref's range (citation_sweep.py) or the row's span (check_marks.py) happens to include a true site elsewhere. This is the review's primary finding (T1-01, T1-02). Separately, the adjacent-negation rule can in principle misread a double-negation phrasing (T1-03), but no such phrasing exists in the real corpus, so that is a latent, not observed, risk, and it runs in the false-positive (over-flagging) rather than false-negative direction.
answers.q4: Sound. A ketiv/qere claim resting on an OSHB editorial note (rather than the kq inventory) requires BOTH that the note's own text match KQ_NOTE (ketib/qere/K-Q wording) AND that the claim's local tail/context carry NOTE_WORD ('notes'/'editorial') language - tested by cs_kq_editorial_note_ok (passes) and cs_kq_none_bad (correctly fails) in the existing suite, both GREEN. I did not find a path for a note-tier ketiv/qere claim to pass without both byte support and terminology support.
answers.q5: Correct and thoroughly verified independently of prose. The zone predicates (web_pairs_in_offset_zone / mt_pairs_in_offset_zone) were exhaustively property-tested against ezek_lib's crosswalk for every one of the 1273 WEB verses and every one of the 1273 MT verses (_test_zone_tools_ezek.py, GREEN). web_mt_offset_map.json independently reports verdict GREEN with its own three checks (round-trip both directions, injectivity). build_verse_maps.py's seam asserts pin all four zone-boundary transitions and the two zone-edge identity points explicitly. No defect found in this area.
answers.q6: Lossless by the tool's own unconditional design (an assertion aborts the run if any original leaf string fails to survive verbatim in the view), and digest-pinned to the exact input file (aborts on any drift from the pinned SHA256) - I read but, per the brief, did not run this tool, since it writes under SP. Its Hebrew copy (_view_ref_hebrew) is correctly bound to its originating ref, source, and disclosure fields as one string per entry. The tool's own docstring/manifest openly discloses one limitation: a disclosure copied beside its Hebrew can be double-counted by FLAGS-tier members that walk every string - this only inflates a triage count (never hides a real finding) and does not touch HARD/RED members, so it cannot mask a hard defect.
answers.q7: The deterministic counts are internally consistent and I verified two of them by direct arithmetic against the real run's output: the citation_sweep by_part breakdown sums to exactly 546 (matching 'problems': 546), and the by_class breakdown also sums to exactly 546. orchestrator_observations does not overclaim - every judgment-tier block is explicitly hedged ('a listed line is a candidate for review, not a verdict', 'Each item needs a reader; none is a verdict', 'it rules on nothing'), and the tool cleanly separates deterministic tallies from its own reading. No overclaiming found.
answers.q8: The missing adversarial case is exactly T1-01/T1-02: a puncta claim naming an explicitly WRONG verse number, embedded in a ref range or row span that happens to also cover a true site (41:20 or 46:22). The existing PUNCTA2_CS/PUNCTA2_CM vectors test 'range covers site + correct number named' and 'span covers site + no number named' but never 'covers site + wrong number named' - I wrote and ran exactly that vector in my own private scratch (see private_vectors_run) and it exposed the defect in both tools.
answers.q9: The great majority of TOOLKIT.md's factual claims are mechanically asserted and were independently confirmed GREEN by running ezek_lib.py's own selftest (32/32: chapter/verse totals, crosswalk injectivity and round-trip, zone-pair agreement, KJV-variance corroboration, parashah/paseq/K-Q/puncta counts and sites, kq_split's exact method distribution with its two named regressions). I additionally spot-verified the twice-corrected ch-40 K/Q cluster claim directly against Ezek_oshb.txt bytes and confirmed it is now accurate. I could not independently verify the 'PROPHETIC FRAME SPINE' formula/dateline verse-counts (they rest on ezek_device_inventory.json, which is not in this brief's pinned artifact table, so I did not open it) - recorded under unresolved_uncertainty rather than confirmed or refuted. The 'staged tools' table's one-line PUNCTA description is accurate as far as it states, but does not claim (and so is not falsified by) the exclusivity gap found in T1-01/T1-02.
